overview: The Añú, also called Paraujano, are an Indigenous people of northwestern Venezuela, with communities around Sinamaica Lagoon and elsewhere in Zulia. Fishing, waterside homes and family relationships connect everyday life with the lagoon. Their language belongs to the Arawak family, while recent community projects document efforts to sustain knowledge across generations.

periods.title: Research on family relationships
periods.summary: Rosales published a study describing flexible kinship and residential ties at Sinamaica. Relationships extended across households through marriage, shared services and celebrations.

periods.title: A community language initiative
periods.summary: A UNICEF partnership with MOCUPA supported a center at Sinamaica. The 2001 review described elders teaching children and young community members documenting words, stories and songs.

periods.title: Family knowledge in an educational book
periods.summary: A UNICEF publication brought together observations and conversations with parents, elders and children for use by families and teachers.

periods.title: Describing architecture on the water
periods.summary: Quintero Weir’s thesis explained how mangrove framing and plant materials supported houses, with filled enclosures creating small garden plots beside some homes.

periods.title: Language study and teaching materials
periods.summary: Álvarez described severe language shift and work on learning resources. His assessment belongs to 2009 and does not establish the number of speakers today.

periods.title: Children learning about their rights
periods.summary: UNICEF documented a November activity at a Sinamaica school serving mainly Añú children. Pupils discussed children’s rights in their own community setting.

items.text: The 2006 family study describes fishing with nets, basket traps and wooden traps, supplying food and products for sale. Salting helped preserve catches. Some families close to land also tended coconut and plantain plots, while purchased goods linked households to nearby towns. The account describes particular communities rather than an unchanging way of life for every Añú family.

Mangrove poles form the supports and framework of houses raised over the water. Quintero Weir describes a floor about a meter and a half above the surface, with woven enea and majagua plant materials forming walls and roofing. The building method depends on selecting different sizes of wood for different parts of the structure.

Some families created garden space beside a principal household by enclosing an area with mangrove poles, then adding alternating layers of river sediment and coconut husks or shells. These small raised plots show how people made cultivable ground within a watery environment. The thesis calls them escolleras or chinampas; it does not say every household had one.

Rosales’s kinship study describes people maintaining ties to more than one residential group. Marriage connections, bilateral kin relationships, celebrations and exchanges of services helped sustain solidarity. This makes the household part of a wider social network, rather than a completely separate unit defined only by one dwelling.

The study also emphasizes relative age in kinship terminology. Words for relatives carry expectations about relationships and conduct, rather than simply listing biological connections. Its account is a particular researcher’s interpretation of the community studied, not a rule that every family must follow in the same way.

A center supported through MOCUPA gave older women a place to speak Añú with children and young people. The 2001 evaluation describes the sharing of language and customs remembered from earlier generations. Elders appear here as teachers and contributors to a community project, rather than merely as subjects interviewed by outside researchers.

The same evaluation reports that six young community promoters helped collect more than 3,000 words, fifteen stories and five songs. These are reported documentation outputs, not a count of fluent speakers or proof that ordinary transmission had been restored. Keeping stories and songs alongside vocabulary preserved different forms of expression.

Álvarez prepared learning materials at the invitation of MOCUPA and ASINDIAÑU. Earlier records, including Marie-France Patte’s fieldwork from 1973 to 1981, were essential resources when few speakers remained available. His article distinguishes collected evidence from the editorial work needed to turn it into teaching material.

Vowel length distinguishes sounds in Añú. Álvarez discusses how a practical writing system represents those contrasts, an important detail for teaching the language accurately. The language is related to Wayuunaiki, but that relationship does not make the two languages or peoples interchangeable.

On 20 November 2024, girls at a Sinamaica school serving predominantly Añú children took part in a discussion about children’s rights, documented in UNICEF’s activity report. This is a dated example of contemporary community life. It does not establish that all educational or language needs have been met.

ending.text: The Añú did not disappear when this map entry ends in 1500. Modern community studies and the documented 2024 school activity show continuing life at Sinamaica. Language loss and efforts to teach younger generations form part of that history; they should not be confused with the extinction of a people.
